text.p: These are the leading stories in the Kenyan press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Police are investigating a mysterious explosion that killed a computer programmer and destroyed crucial records in the government Central Bureau of Statistics offices in Nairobi.
- The Pest Control Products Board is building a 919 million shilling headquarters on the edge of Nairobi, with approval from neither the treasury nor the parent ministry of agriculture.

- Opposition parliament member says weekend attack on the Dutch and British envoys by three cabinet ministers was meant to divert attention from the "ills of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party government".

- Opposition parliamentarian Njenga Mungai says confessions by a former Nakuru councillor and an ex-army man that they were guerillas posed a threat to Rift Valley Province leaders' efforts to reconcile different ethnic communities.

- Moslem leaders from North Eastern Province of Kenya say the reform campaign launched by some Western envoys ahead of the next general election was intended to ensure that the political leadership of Kenya was handed over to a select community.
- The Narok district commissioner John Nandasaba cautions that the government will not tolerate leaders who incite the various Maasai clans to fight over land disputes.
- Regional nations consult informally on an announcement by the military government in Burundi that it is restoring parliament and lifting a two-month-old ban on political parties.
- Ugandan government summons Kenyan High Commissioner Peter Ole Njuraiyia to explain Uganda's position on claims Ugandan officials had given armed and logistical support to Kenyan rebels.

- The liquidation of the Heritage Bank sees four Kenyan public institutions lose 332 million shillings ($5.6 million) of the total 388 million shillings ($6.8 million) bad loans the organisation advanced to three large borrowers after it was re-opened in May 1995.
